claim: Gene copy number is a key factor controlling RNAi for transcripts from endogenous loci.
source: Here we have used a synthetic RNAi system to show that gene copy number is a key factor controlling RNAi for transcripts from endogenous loci, since transcripts from multi-copy loci form double stranded RNA more efficiently than transcripts from equivalently expressed single-copy loci.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as a main finding of the study, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Transcripts from multi-copy loci form double stranded RNA more efficiently than transcripts from equivalently expressed single-copy loci.
source: Here we have used a synthetic RNAi system to show that gene copy number is a key factor controlling RNAi for transcripts from endogenous loci, since transcripts from multi-copy loci form double stranded RNA more efficiently than transcripts from equivalently expressed single-copy loci.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5D showing RNase A resistance.

claim: Selectivity towards transcripts from high-copy DNA is an emergent property of a minimal RNAi system.
source: Selectivity towards transcripts from high-copy DNA is therefore an emergent property of a minimal RNAi system.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by genome-wide analysis in Figure 4.

claim: Low-level genome-wide pervasive transcription is sufficient to instigate RNAi.
source: We show that low-level genome-wide pervasive transcription is sufficient to instigate RNAi, and propose that pervasive transcription is part of a defense mechanism capable of directing a sequence-independent RNAi response against transposable elements amplifying within the genome.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally with the GAL cluster in Figure 8.

claim: Pervasive transcription is part of a defense mechanism capable of directing a sequence-independent RNAi response against transposable elements amplifying within the genome.
source: We show that low-level genome-wide pervasive transcription is sufficient to instigate RNAi, and propose that pervasive transcription is part of a defense mechanism capable of directing a sequence-independent RNAi response against transposable elements amplifying within the genome.
evidence: This is proposed as a hypothesis based on the experimental findings and logical inference.

claim: 15-30% of yeast open reading frames have an annotated antisense ncRNA depending on the minimum size of overlap considered.
source: Combining published datasets we found that 15–30% of yeast open reading frames (ORFs) have an annotated antisense ncRNA depending on the minimum size of overlap considered (Xu et al., 2009; van Dijk et al., 2011), not including overlapping convergent ORFs (Figure 1B and Table 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of published datasets as shown in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: ORFs with annotated antisense ncRNAs produce more siRNA than ORFs lacking an antisense in RNAi+ cells.
source: In RNAi+ cells, these ORFs produce more siRNA than ORFs lacking an antisense (Figure 1C), showing that they are transcribed into dsRNA that is targeted by the RNAi machinery.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of sequencing data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ORFs with antisense ncRNAs do not show reduced mRNA levels in RNAi+ cells.
source: However, these ORFs do not show reduced mRNA levels in RNAi+ cells consistent with published data, suggesting that insufficient siRNAs are produced to elicit a detectable mRNA knockdown (Derrien et al., 2012; Katayama et al., 2005; Drinnenberg et al., 2011) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D and is consistent with published literature.

claim: Approximately 90% of yeast antisense RNAs are highly unstable.
source: As for approximately 90% of yeast antisense RNAs (Table 1), MAL32 antisense RNA is highly unstable and is only detectable in strains lacking the nuclear exosome co-factor Trf4 (reviewed in Houseley and Tollervey, 2009) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: Y′ element ncRNAs from both strands are largely absent in RNAi+ strains, being replaced by heterogeneous degradation products and readily detectable siRNAs.
source: Northern blots revealed full-length ncRNAs from both strands of the Y′ elements in wild-type cells (Figure 2B lanes 1,5 marked with arrows); these were largely absent in the RNAi+ strain, being replaced by heterogeneous degradation products and readily detectable siRNAs (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the northern blot data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: rDNA intergenic spacer ncRNAs are degraded by RNAi in a similar manner to Y′ element ncRNAs.
source: Equivalent results were seen for the rDNA intergenic spacer region (Figure 2D–F). These data show that endo-siRNA pairs can form RNAi substrates and undergo efficient degradation by a minimal RNAi system.
evidence: This is demonstrated by northern blot analysis in Figure 2D-F.

claim: Endogenous MAL32 mRNA was not down-regulated in RNAi+ trf4Δ cells.
source: MAL32 antisense RNA is highly unstable and is only detectable in strains lacking the nuclear exosome co-factor Trf4 (reviewed in Houseley and Tollervey, 2009) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), but endogenous MAL32 mRNA was not down-regulated in the RNAi+ strain even in trf4Δ cells (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown by northern blot analysis in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: MAL32 mRNA was significantly down-regulated by RNAi when expressed from a high-copy plasmid.
source: When expressed from a high-copy plasmid, however, MAL32 mRNA was significantly down-regulated by RNAi (Figure 3C) with concurrent production of siRNA (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by northern blot analysis in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: The knockdown of MAL32 mRNA represents a genuine RNAi response requiring both Dicer and Argonaute.
source: To confirm that the knockdown of MAL32 mRNA was not an indirect effect of the strain background or an undirected Argonaute cleavage, we reconstituted the RNAi system in the BY4741 background using separate plasmids expressing Dicer and Argonaute. dsRNA from the MAL32 locus was detectable in these cells and was removed by Dicer; however, a significant knockdown of the mRNA was only observed in cells expressing both Dicer and Argonaute, confirming that the knockdown represents a genuine RNAi response (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: GAL4 mRNA was not significantly decreased in full-length RNA in RNAi+ xrn1Δ cells at the endogenous locus.
source: Cells lacking Xrn1 show increased levels of antisense and, unexpectedly, sense RNA, but, as for MAL32, we did not detect a significant decrease in full-length RNA in RNAi+ xrn1Δ cells (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown by northern blot analysis in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Amplification of the GAL4 locus by cloning on a high-copy plasmid leads to significant degradation of the sense RNA along with the antisense RNA by RNAi.
source: However, amplification of the locus by cloning on a high-copy plasmid leads to significant degradation of the sense RNA along with the antisense RNA by RNAi (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by northern blot analysis in Figure 3G and 3H.

claim: RNAi+ cells contained approximately twofold more high-copy plasmid than the controls.
source: However, Southern blotting revealed that RNAi+ cells contained approximately twofold more plasmid than the controls, which would tend to decrease rather than increase the apparent effect of RNAi (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Southern blot analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A,B.

claim: MAL32 mRNA was knocked down approximately 75% in RNAi+ cells as measured by dsRNA immunoprecipitation and qRT-PCR.
source: MAL32 mRNA was knocked down approximately 75%, as observed by northern blot analysis, while dsRNA was reduced 11-fold, consistent with specific removal of dsRNA by Dicer.
evidence: This is demonstrated by dsRNA immunoprecipitation and qRT-PCR shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: GAL4 mRNA knockdown was measured at 80% in RNAi+ cells by dsRNA immunoprecipitation and qRT-PCR.
source: GAL4 mRNA knockdown was measured at 80% in this assay, again with an 11-fold reduction in dsRNA in the RNAi+ strain (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dsRNA immunoprecipitation and qRT-PCR shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Multi-copy loci produce more siRNA than single-copy loci with equivalent RNA abundance.
source: siRNA production was significantly higher from multi-copy loci than from single-copy loci in all except the lowest category of RNA abundance. This result was robust to changes in the threshold between low and high copy, and was still observed in a comparison of low to medium copy number, showing that high-copy Ty1 retrotransposons were not distorting the analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genome-wide analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The 1% of genome with the highest siRNA:total RNA ratio is massively enriched for multi-copy loci.
source: As predicted, the 1% of genome with the highest siRNA:total RNA ratio is massively enriched for multi-copy loci (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There is a correlation between regions of high-copy number and regions with high siRNA:total RNA abundance across a chromosome.
source: when this ratio was plotted across a chromosome, an obvious correlation was observed between regions of high-copy number and regions with high siRNA:total RNA abundance (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The clustered TRP1 system produced fourfold more TRP1 siRNA than the dispersed system despite similar amounts of sense and antisense RNA molecules.
source: Quantification of total RNA showed that both systems produced similar amounts of sense and antisense RNA molecules (Figure 6B), although this experiment was complicated by read-through transcripts of antisense TRP1 from the clustered system (Figure 6B lanes 1,2), a behavior that was not prevented by insertion of transcriptional stop cassettes between the repeats. Nonetheless, the clustered system produced fourfold more TRP1 siRNA than the dispersed system (Figure 6C), showing that close nuclear juxtaposition of transcriptional loci enhances dsRNA formation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by northern blot analysis in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Close nuclear juxtaposition of transcriptional loci enhances dsRNA formation.
source: Nonetheless, the clustered system produced fourfold more TRP1 siRNA than the dispersed system (Figure 6C), showing that close nuclear juxtaposition of transcriptional loci enhances dsRNA formation.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental comparison of clustered and dispersed TRP1 systems shown in Figure 6.

claim: Low abundance sense-antisense ncRNA pairs undergo efficient RNAi when amplified to high copy number.
source: While testing the effects of copy number amplification on siRNA production, we noticed that even low abundance sense-antisense ncRNA pairs (selected from a published dataset, Xu et al., 2009) underwent efficient RNAi when amplified to high copy number.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated with SUT176 and SUT430 systems in Figure 7.

claim: SUT176 and SUT430 sense and antisense RNAs are barely detectable by northern blot and are clearly not targeted for degradation by RNAi at single-copy.
source: For both the SUT176 and SUT430 systems (Figure 7A), the sense and antisense RNAs are barely detectable by northern blot and are clearly not targeted for degradation by RNAi (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by northern blot analysis in Figure 7B.

claim: After cloning on high-copy plasmids, SUT176 and SUT430 full-length RNAs became highly susceptible to RNAi and produced copious siRNAs.
source: However, after cloning on high-copy plasmids, the full-length RNAs became highly susceptible to RNAi and produced copious siRNAs (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by northern blot analysis in Figure 7C and 7D.

claim: Antisense ncRNAs are produced from the GAL10 ORF with a known steady-state abundance of one RNA molecule per 14 cells in cells grown in glucose.
source: Under these conditions, antisense ncRNAs are produced from the GAL10 ORF with a known steady-state abundance of one RNA molecule per 14 cells (Houseley et al., 2008; Pinskaya et al., 2009) (arrows in Figure 8B lane 1).
evidence: This is stated based on published literature and shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The RBSΔ RNAi+ strain only produces very low level heterogeneous transcripts from GAL10, forming a good model of pervasive transcription.
source: Nonetheless, the RBSΔ RNAi+ strain (Figure 8B lane 4) only produces very low level heterogeneous transcripts from GAL10, suggesting that it forms a good model of pervasive transcription.
evidence: This is stated based on the northern blot analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: ncRNAs produced at the level of pervasive transcription are sufficient to mediate extensive siRNA production when the copy number of the transcribing locus is increased.
source: Cloning either wild-type or RBSΔ GAL clusters onto high-copy plasmids substantially increased the levels of detectable ncRNA as expected (Figure 8B lanes 5,7), and these ncRNAs were processed into easily detectable siRNAs (Figure 8C lanes 6,8). Therefore, ncRNAs produced at the level of pervasive transcription are sufficient to mediate extensive siRNA production when the copy number of the transcribing locus is increased.
evidence: This is demonstrated by northern blot analysis in Figure 8B and 8C.

claim: Both wild-type and RBSΔ high-copy GAL cluster plasmids caused highly significant >50% knockdowns of the GAL10 mRNA expressed from a single-copy locus.
source: As observed for the GAL10 ncRNAs, the GAL10 mRNA was expressed at higher levels in the RNAi+ strain than in the wild-type (Figure 8D compare lanes 1,2) but, nonetheless, both wild-type and RBSΔ high-copy GAL cluster plasmids caused highly significant >50% knockdowns of the GAL10 mRNA compared with the empty vector control (Figure 8D lanes 2,4,6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by northern blot analysis in Figure 8D.

claim: Pervasive transcription of a high-copy locus is sufficient to instigate an effective RNAi response that can mediate the degradation of a target mRNA in trans.
source: These data demonstrate that pervasive transcription of a high-copy locus is sufficient to instigate an effective RNAi response that can mediate the degradation of a target mRNA in trans.
evidence: This is concluded from the GAL10 knockdown experiments shown in Figure 8D.

claim: RNAi has an innate preference for the products of high-copy sequences, probably because RNA from high-copy sequences forms dsRNA more efficiently.
source: Here we have demonstrated that RNAi has an innate preference for the products of high-copy sequences, probably because RNA from high-copy sequences forms dsRNA more efficiently.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion in the Discussion section, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: RNAi provides a mechanism to differentiate high- and low-copy regions by selectively targeting the products of high-copy loci.
source: This of course requires a mechanism to count copy number, or at least differentiate high- and low-copy regions, which has remained mysterious. Our data show that RNAi provides such a mechanism by selectively targeting the products of high-copy loci.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: The production of siRNA from high-copy DNA requires that all DNA is transcribed.
source: The production of siRNA from high-copy DNA, which would be the basis of such a counting mechanism, absolutely requires that all DNA is transcribed; if this does not occur, transposable elements that remain transcriptionally silent would be invisible to the system.
evidence: This is stated as a logical requirement in the Discussion section.

claim: Pervasive transcription ensures that the vast majority of the genome is transcribed, and therefore that no region remains completely silent.
source: Pervasive transcription, the general background of very low level RNA produced across the genome, ensures that the vast majority of the genome is transcribed, and therefore that no region remains completely silent (Cheng et al., 2005; Birney et al., 2007; Kapranov et al., 2007; Goodman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The ENCODE project found that almost all the human genome is transcribed at some point, but the products of this transcription are vanishingly rare.
source: More mysterious is the pervasive transcription that permeates eukaryotic genomes; the ENCODE project found that almost all the human genome is transcribed at some point, but the products of this transcription are vanishingly rare (Cheng et al., 2005; Birney et al., 2007; Kapranov et al., 2007; Goodman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated based on published ENCODE project findings.

claim: The primary function of pervasive transcription lies in ensuring the whole genome is transcribed to allow identification and suppression of transposable elements.
source: We suggest that the primary function of pervasive transcription lies in ensuring the whole genome is transcribed to allow identification and suppression of transposable elements; this does not conflict with the idea that some proportion of these transcripts may have additional functions.
evidence: This is proposed as a hypothesis in the Discussion section based on the experimental findings.

claim: The rate of formation of dsRNA from single stranded sense and antisense RNA is proportional to the concentration of each strand of RNA, and so is inversely proportional to the square of the reaction volume.
source: We propose that hybridization kinetics explains the dependence of RNAi on copy number (shown in Figure 9). The rate of formation of dsRNA from single stranded sense and antisense RNA is proportional to the concentration of each strand of RNA, and so is inversely proportional to the square of the reaction volume.
evidence: This is stated as a mechanistic explanation in the Discussion section based on chemical kinetics principles.

claim: Single-copy loci cannot simultaneously transcribe sense and antisense RNA.
source: Single-copy loci cannot simultaneously transcribe sense and antisense RNA (Hobson et al., 2012) so, although such a locus can give rise to a mixed population of sense and antisense RNA in the cytoplasm over time, in the vicinity of the transcription site only one sense of RNA should ever be present, assuming efficient RNA export.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: At multi-copy loci the simultaneous production of sense and antisense RNA from many closely spaced sites can lead to high concentrations of sense and antisense RNA around the transcription site, causing efficient duplex formation and hence efficient RNAi.
source: In contrast, at multi-copy loci the simultaneous production of sense and antisense RNA from many closely spaced sites can lead to high concentrations of sense and antisense RNA around the transcription site, causing efficient duplex formation and hence efficient RNAi.
evidence: This is stated as a mechanistic explanation in the Discussion section.

claim: Dicer is largely cytoplasmic in higher eukaryotes, but small quantities of nuclear Dicer have been detected, particularly associated with chromatin.
source: This reflects the situation in higher eukaryotes where Dicer is largely cytoplasmic, but recent experiments in Drosophila and mammalian cells have detected small quantities of nuclear Dicer, particularly associated with chromatin (Sinkkonen et al., 2010; Cernilogar et al., 2011; Gullerova et al., 2011; Doyle et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: All the systems described in this paper that undergo efficient RNAi are clustered: rDNA repeats are arranged in tandem, telomeres cluster together at various points in the cell cycle, and high-copy 2µ plasmids exist in a discrete focus.
source: One notable prediction of this mechanism is that clustering of multi-copy transcription sites would be a particularly efficient way to increase the local density of sense and antisense RNA. All the systems we have described in this paper are clustered: rDNA repeats are arranged in tandem, telomeres are known to cluster together at various points in the cell cycle (Gotta et al., 1996), and high-copy 2µ plasmids exist in a discrete focus that is vital for copy number maintenance (Velmurugan et al., 2000; Wong et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Tf2 retrotransposons in Schizosaccharomyces pombe are clustered by the action of centromere protein B (CENP-B), which also silences these elements through histone deacetylation.
source: Intriguingly, Tf2 retrotransposons in Schizosaccharomyces pombe are clustered by the action of centromere protein B (CENP-B), which also silences these elements through histone deacetylation (Cam et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: Gypsy retrotransposons in Drosophila are known to cluster.
source: Similarly, gypsy retrotransposons in Drosophila are known to cluster (Gerasimova et al., 2000), which may again facilitate siRNA production.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: siRNAs in mammalian sperm and oocytes show a pronounced bias towards high-copy sequences.
source: Mammalian germline cells are replete with small RNAs including endogenous siRNA (Watanabe et al., 2006, 2008; Tam et al., 2008; Song et al., 2011), and siRNAs in sperm and oocytes show a pronounced bias towards high-copy sequences that would be effectively explained by the selectivity of the RNAi system towards the products of high-copy loci (Watanabe et al., 2006; Song et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Transgenic mice expressing a hairpin dsRNA construct produce minimal siRNAs, little edited RNA, and show no phenotype that might indicate cell death.
source: However, transgenic mice expressing a hairpin dsRNA construct produce minimal siRNAs, little edited RNA, and show no phenotype that might indicate cell death (Nejepinska et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: siRNAs produced from LINE-1 retrotransposons have been detected in mammalian cell culture.
source: Nonetheless, siRNAs produced from LINE-1 retrotransposons have been detected in cell culture (Yang and Kazazian, 2006), and high-copy transfected plasmids expressing a sense-antisense RNA pair do produce detectable siRNA in HEK293 cells (Nejepinska et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: A basic siRNA response with an apparent bias towards high-copy sequences is functional in mammalian somatic cells.
source: This shows that a basic siRNA response with an apparent bias towards high-copy sequences is functional in mammalian somatic cells.
evidence: This is concluded in the Discussion section based on cited literature.

claim: S. cerevisiae is highly unusual in lacking an endogenous RNAi system, allowing maintenance of the symbiotic dsRNA Killer virus.
source: S. cerevisiae is highly unusual in lacking an endogenous RNAi system, allowing maintenance of the symbiotic dsRNA Killer virus (Drinnenberg et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction section and supported by a citation.

claim: The reconstituted RNAi system in S. cerevisiae efficiently degrades exogenous hairpin RNAs and endogenous Ty retrotransposon transcripts.
source: The reconstituted system is functional, since RNAi+ S. cerevisiae efficiently degrades exogenous hairpin RNAs and endogenous Ty retrotransposon transcripts; however, no clear mRNA expression changes are detectable in these cells (Drinnenberg et al., 2009, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction section and supported by citations.

claim: No clear mRNA expression changes are detectable in RNAi+ S. cerevisiae cells.
source: The reconstituted system is functional, since RNAi+ S. cerevisiae efficiently degrades exogenous hairpin RNAs and endogenous Ty retrotransposon transcripts; however, no clear mRNA expression changes are detectable in these cells (Drinnenberg et al., 2009, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction section and supported by citations.

claim: Protein-coding mRNAs are augmented by a multitude of non-protein coding RNAs, many produced from regions of the genome traditionally considered to be transcriptionally silent.
source: Genome-wide sequencing studies in many organisms have revealed that protein-coding mRNAs are augmented by a multitude of non-protein coding RNAs (ncRNAs), many produced from regions of the genome traditionally considered to be transcriptionally silent (The ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012; Bertone et al., 2004; Cheng et al., 2005; David et al., 2006; Birney et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction section and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Functional data for the vast majority of ncRNAs are currently lacking.
source: Functional data for the vast majority of ncRNAs are currently lacking, with only a few examples characterized in any detail; however, the diversity of mechanisms by which these act suggests that ncRNAs have a rich and varied biology that is largely still to be sampled.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction section as general knowledge about the field.

claim: Long ncRNAs which overlap protein-coding genes have the potential to modulate the expression of their cognate coding RNA.
source: Long ncRNAs which overlap protein-coding genes have the potential to modulate the expression of their cognate coding RNA.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction section as a general principle.

claim: The vast majority of ncRNAs in budding yeast are unstable.
source: The vast majority of ncRNAs in budding yeast are unstable (Neil et al., 2009; van Dijk et al., 2011), limiting the potential action of the RNAs themselves, although the transcription of such RNAs can still alter gene expression (reviewed in Houseley, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction section and supported by citations.

claim: RNAi probably evolved to protect cells against dsRNA viruses, a role which is maintained in plants, insects, and lower eukaryotes.
source: RNAi probably evolved to protect cells against dsRNA viruses, a role which is maintained in plants, insects, and lower eukaryotes (Ding, 2010) and has recently been described in mammalian cells (Li et al., 2013; Maillard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction section and supported by citations.

claim: RNAi forms a potent defense against transposons, and high-copy transposon-derived sequences are excellent targets for RNAi, giving rise to copious siRNAs in most eukaryotes including mammals.
source: RNAi also forms a potent defense against transposons, and high-copy transposon-derived sequences are excellent targets for RNAi, giving rise to copious siRNAs in most eukaryotes including mammals (Yang and Kazazian, 2006; Slotkin and Martienssen, 2007; Babiarz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction section and supported by citations.

claim: siRNAs can mediate transcriptional repression of target RNAs through chromatin modifications and DNA methylation, although this activity is seemingly much stronger in lower eukaryotes and plants than in mammals.
source: In addition to degrading transposon-derived and viral RNA, siRNAs can mediate transcriptional repression of target RNAs through chromatin modifications and DNA methylation, although this activity is seemingly much stronger in lower eukaryotes and plants than in mammals (Martienssen et al., 2005; Lejeune et al., 2010; Zhang and Zhu, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction section and supported by citations.

claim: Efficient generation of siRNAs from endogenous sense-antisense systems has been observed in plants under stress.
source: Efficient generation of siRNAs from endogenous sense-antisense systems (endo-siRNA) has been observed in plants under stress (Borsani et al., 2005; Katiyar-Agarwal et al., 2006), and mammalian oocytes generate endo-siRNAs that can mediate mRNA knockdown (Tam et al., 2008; Watanabe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction section and supported by citations.

claim: Mammalian oocytes generate endo-siRNAs that can mediate mRNA knockdown.
source: Efficient generation of siRNAs from endogenous sense-antisense systems (endo-siRNA) has been observed in plants under stress (Borsani et al., 2005; Katiyar-Agarwal et al., 2006), and mammalian oocytes generate endo-siRNAs that can mediate mRNA knockdown (Tam et al., 2008; Watanabe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction section and supported by citations.

claim: endo-siRNAs are surprisingly under-represented where sense and antisense RNAs are co-expressed in mammalian somatic cells.
source: However, although endo-siRNAs have been detected outside the germline in mammals, they are surprisingly under-represented where sense and antisense RNAs are co-expressed (Faghihi and Wahlestedt, 2006; Okamura et al., 2008; Carlile et al., 2009)
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction section and supported by citations.

claim: There is a positive correlation between antisense and sense RNA expression in mammalian genomes, which is inconsistent with RNAi.
source: and overall there is a positive correlation between antisense and sense RNA expression in mammalian genomes, which is inconsistent with RNAi (Derrien et al., 2012; Katayama et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction section and supported by citations.
